L15: cite3†Company L16: # Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence
L17: 
L18: Loading…

L21: On August 28, we began training a new internal model. In addition to cite4†resolving the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem⁠ , this model has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics. The cite5†pace of its progress⁠ in mathematics has surprised the mathematicians within OpenAI. This has led to internal discussions on the best way to inform the community of the rapid progress to prepare and adapt the field.
L22: Mathematics is a fundamental science, and novel discoveries may result in a wide range of applications. That makes the promise of these capabilities substantial, and their responsible development and deployment important beyond mathematics itself. We recognize this and are working through how broader deployment of math-related AI capabilities can be done responsibly.
L23: In a recent open letter “cite6†A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics⁠(opens in a new window)†mathandai.org ,” mathematicians raise concerns about the negative externalities of solving open problems as a benchmark for new AI systems.
L24: Their criticisms highlight the need for thoughtful engagement of AI companies with the math community. To that end, we’re working with mathematicians who have established an independent mathematics advisory group. This group will serve as a bridge to the mathematical community and broader public, giving mathematicians a voice in how we move forward.
L25: The group will advise on the review and communication of emerging results: they will help OpenAI assess their significance, advise on how to coordinate their dissemination, and advise on academic and professional standards of mathematical research. It will also advise on how our tools can support mathematical research and learning. We want to put capable tools in mathematicians’ hands so they can pursue the questions they know best and develop new ideas.
L26: The group will operate independently from OpenAI. The group will have the freedom to offer advice we have not requested, comment on OpenAI’s impact on mathematics, and make its advice public. Its value depends on its members being able to exercise their own judgement and challenge ours. Its members will not be paid by OpenAI, and the group can change its membership as it sees fit. Importantly, the group will not be responsible for advising us on how to pace our internal progress on mathematics.
L27: Working with this group is a first step. There are difficult questions ahead about how AI can support mathematical understanding and how the benefits of these capabilities can reach the wider community. We want mathematicians to be at the center of shaping the answers.
L28:

L15: cite3†Company L16: # Expanding OpenAI Academy with new learning paths
L17: 
L18: Role-based learning helps employees, developers, leaders, educators, and students build practical AI skills and demonstrate what they’ve learned.
L19:

L27:   * cite5†Choose a learning path for the work you do L28:     * cite6†Knowledge workers: Apply AI at Work L29:     * cite7†Developers: Build with AI L30:     * cite8†Leaders: Lead AI Adoption L31:     * cite9†Educators and students: Teach and Learn with AI L32:   * cite10†Bring OpenAI Academy courses to your organization L33:   * cite5†Choose a learning path for the work you do L34:     * cite6†Knowledge workers: Apply AI at Work L35:     * cite7†Developers: Build with AI L36:     * cite8†Leaders: Lead AI Adoption L37:     * cite9†Educators and students: Teach and Learn with AI L38:   * cite10†Bring OpenAI Academy courses to your organization L39: 
L40: Using AI safely and effectively takes practice. People need to learn how to apply it to the work in front of them, whether they’re improving a daily workflow, building a product, leading a team, or teaching a class.
L41: At OpenAI, we treat learning as part of deployment. Today, we’re expanding OpenAI Academy with new courses for developers, leaders, educators, and college students. These join Apply AI at Work, which helps people build foundational skills, create repeatable workflows, and direct work with agents.
L42: Together, the pathways help organizations build shared habits for working with AI and develop the skills different roles require. Course assessments give learners a way to demonstrate what they’ve learned. Learners earn an OpenAI Academy course badge by passing the course assessment.
L43: ## Choose a learning path for the work you do
L44: 
L45: cite11†OpenAI Academy ⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com courses are built around a simple idea: you should use AI to learn AI. Learners practice on real tasks, giving instructions, adding context, and reviewing results as they go.
L46: 
L47: Organizations can combine Apply AI at Work with focused learning for developers, leaders, educators, and students, choosing the courses that support their teams’ work.
L48: ### Knowledge workers: Apply AI at Work
L49: 
L50: The cite12†Apply AI at Work⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com pathway helps people use AI more effectively in their everyday work. Learners start with the basics, practicing how to give clear instructions, add relevant context, and review responses against the task at hand. They then turn successful approaches into workflows they can reuse.
L51: As learners progress, they practice directing larger pieces of work with agents, deciding what to delegate and where to add checkpoints and human review. The pathway helps employees take on more complex tasks with AI while retaining responsibility for the final result.
L52: ### Developers: Build with AI
L53: The cite13†Build with AI⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com pathway is designed for developers and technical teams using Codex or building products with the OpenAI API. For developers, the courses cover how to plan and implement changes across the software development lifecycle while maintaining control over review and quality. For teams building on the API, the pathway covers solution design, evaluations, agents, retrieving relevant information, and operating AI systems in production.
L54: These courses are designed to help organizations move from experimentation to useful, reliable AI systems.
L55: ### Leaders: Lead AI Adoption
L56: 
L57: Leaders must also decide where AI can create meaningful value, what the organization should prioritize, who owns the work, and how progress will be measured.
L58: The cite14†AI Leadership⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com course, part of cite15†Lead AI Adoption⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com , helps people responsible for strategy, adoption, and change management assess where AI could create business value. Learners connect an initiative to business priorities, define ownership and governance, and develop an initial AI strategy and roadmap for adoption.
L59: ### Educators and students: Teach and Learn with AI
L60: 
L61: cite16†AI for Educators⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com and cite17†AI for College Students⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com extend the portfolio to teaching, learning, and career preparation.
L62: In AI for Educators, learners use materials they have permission to use to plan a class, create an activity or assessment, or adapt communications for students, teaching assistants, or colleagues. They review ChatGPT’s responses against their learning objectives, source materials, and requirements. The educator decides what belongs in their teaching.
L63: AI for College Students focuses on academic and career tasks. Students practice organizing readings and deadlines into a study plan, assigning roles in a group project, reviewing a draft against assignment requirements, and preparing for applications or interviews. They learn to bring the right materials into ChatGPT, strengthen their work, and make decisions about the final result.
L64: ## Bring OpenAI Academy courses to your organization
L65: 
L66: Organizations can choose the learning paths that match their goals. A company might use Apply AI at Work in employee onboarding, offer Build with AI courses to developers and technical teams, and include AI Leadership in an executive, Champion, or transformation program. Education institutions can combine cite18†AI Foundations⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com with AI for Educators and AI for College Students.
L67: Learning is most useful when people have time to practice and apply it. Managers and Champions can encourage learners to bring real tasks into the courses, share useful examples, and connect what they learn to work already underway.
L68: 
L69: The cite19†OpenAI Academy Deployment Guide⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com includes recommendations for introducing the courses, engaging leaders and managers, building participation, and tracking progress.
L70: The courses are shaped by teams across OpenAI and will continue to be updated as our models, products, and guidance change.
L71: 
L72: Visit cite4†OpenAI Academy⁠(opens in a new window)†academy.openai.com to explore the expanded course portfolio and find the right learning paths for your teams.

L15: cite3†Company L16: # Introducing the Australian Youth Safety Blueprint
L17: 
L18: OpenAI’s approach to protecting, empowering, and creating safer experiences for young people.
L19: 
L20: cite4†Read the blueprint(opens in a new window)†cdn.openai.com L21: 
L22: Loading…
L23: 
L24: Share
L25: We are introducing the cite4†Australian Youth Safety Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window)†cdn.openai.com , a roadmap for protecting young people as they use AI and a practical contribution to the Australian policy landscape. Young Australians deserve tools that expand their opportunities to learn, create, and build skills while protecting their wellbeing.
L26: The Blueprint sets out six pillars, from AI literacy and age-appropriate safeguards to privacy-protective age assurance, connections to real-world crisis support, and accessible parental controls. Together, they help define how responsible AI should work for teens, and how companies should be held accountable for identifying and addressing risks to young people.
L27: We are continuing to strengthen safeguards in our products, informed by these principles. In August, we began rolling out ChatGPT for Teens in Australia, a new default experience for users identified as aged 13 to 17, with updated safeguards designed around their developmental needs. This builds on our parental controls, under-18 safety policies, and age assurance, which helps apply the right protections to the right users.
L28: The responsibility for safety should not fall primarily on young people or their families. Companies must continue to build protections into their products from the outset.
L29: This is ongoing work, and there is more to do. Australia has an opportunity to help shape strong, evidence-based standards that protect young people while preserving access to the benefits of AI. We are committed to learning alongside teens, parents, educators, researchers, and policymakers, and we welcome collaboration from others working towards the same goal.

L44: ## Frontier intelligence for law
L45: 
L46: Astra for Law combines GPT‑6 Astra with a powerful legal search index and instructions for legal analysis and writing. Together, they amplify Astra’s capabilities across the legal practice, while giving firms and legal technology companies the freedom to build their own applications and workflows.
L47: ### Legal research: from facts to a supported answer
L48: 
L49: Our new legal search index is one of the tools Astra for Law can use. Legal research often begins with finding the exact right authority, locating the relevant passages, and understanding how relevant and binding they are to the situation at hand. The index helps Astra for Law do that work, and complements the licensed content and specialist products firms rely on from providers such as Thomson Reuters.
L50: By using the legal search index, Astra for Law can search U.S. case law, statutes, regulations, court rules, and administrative decisions across a corpus of more than 230 million URLs, with sources added daily. Our work with Free Law Project, the nonprofit behind CourtListener, brings its case-law collection covering cite13†more than 99.9% of published U.S. precedential case law⁠(opens in a new window)†wiki.free.law into this research experience.
L51: To measure how this configuration improves legal research, we tested Astra for Law’s complete setup on 200 U.S. legal research questions from the private validation set of cite14†Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window)†vals.ai . This benchmark measures how well the model can find relevant sources and passages, and how well its research answers meet the evaluation criteria.
L52: At the highest reasoning effort for both systems, Astra for Law passed the evaluation’s overall correctness check on 54.0% of questions, compared with 38.7% for GPT‑6 Astra using web search alone – a 40% relative improvement. Astra for Law also produces more comprehensive answers.
L53: On case-law-focused questions, Astra for Law found 24% more reference cases than GPT‑6 Astra using web search alone at the highest reasoning effort. On the audited set of target passages, it retrieved up to 54% more relevant passages from the correct court opinions, when comparing the systems at the same reasoning effort.
L54: 
L55: The result is a stronger research foundation for advising on a deal, assessing a dispute, or developing a legal strategy, with reliable authorities the lawyer can examine for herself.

L57: ### Improving performance on end-to-end legal workflows
L58: 
L59: Legal research is only the first step. Custom instructions for legal analysis and writing guide Astra for Law in applying that research to the client’s facts, developing arguments or deal terms, and identifying weaknesses and uncertainty. That can mean distinguishing a court’s holding from its other observations, addressing cases that weaken an argument, or explaining how a contract exception shifts risk between the parties.
